src.question: A 28-year-old man with a history of injection drug use is evaluated in the emergency department for fever and fatigue. He is cachectic and diaphoretic. His pulse is regular at 110 beats per minute, temperature 38.4 °C (101.1 °F) orally and blood pressure 128/68 mm Hg (right arm, seated). A high-pitched murmur is heard along the left lower sternal border, and small painless hemorrhages are noted on the conjunctivae, palate and palms. What is the recommended initial treatment?
src.key: Begin vancomycin, adjust per blood culture results
src.explanation: Correct. Fever, tachycardia, a new left lower sternal border murmur and painless hemorrhages on the conjunctivae, palate and palms in a person who injects drugs point to endocarditis, most often from Staphylococcus aureus, which may be methicillin-resistant. Vancomycin begins once blood cultures are drawn and is adjusted when the organism and its sensitivities return.

items.html: Streptococcus gallolyticus (bovis) and the colon. Streptococcus gallolyticus comes from the gastrointestinal tract and is associated with liver disease or cirrhosis and with gastrointestinal abnormalities, especially colon cancer. Once the endocarditis is cured, the most important next step is a colonoscopy to look for mucosal lesions.
cites: IE Missing Slide and Cases.pptx, Slides 1, 3

src.question: A 68-year-old man is hospitalized with Streptococcus bovis (gallolyticus) endocarditis of the mitral valve. He recovers completely with appropriate therapy. Which is the most important next step?
src.key: Colonoscopy to look for mucosal lesions
src.explanation: Correct. Streptococcus gallolyticus (bovis) comes from the gastrointestinal tract and is associated with liver disease or cirrhosis and with gastrointestinal abnormalities, especially colon cancer. Once the endocarditis is cured, the most important step is looking for the colonic lesion that let the organism into the blood.

also.explanation: Correct. Streptococcus gallolyticus (bovis) comes from the gastrointestinal tract and is associated with gastrointestinal abnormalities, especially colon cancer, and with liver disease. His new colon cancer, with no dental, urinary or injection source, points to it.

Correct. Streptococcus gallolyticus (bovis) is associated with gastrointestinal abnormalities, especially colon cancer, and with liver disease or cirrhosis. With a normal colonoscopy, liver disease is the other association to keep in mind.

items.html: Culture-negative endocarditis. Culture-negative endocarditis may be due to organisms not recovered by routine microbiology testing or to antimicrobials given before blood cultures were drawn; negative cultures do not exclude endocarditis.
cites: IE Missing Slide and Cases.pptx, Slide 1

src.question: A 55-year-old woman with a bioprosthetic mitral valve placed 4 years ago took a week of oral antibiotics for presumed bronchitis before her fevers were investigated. Three sets of blood cultures now show no growth, but transesophageal echocardiography shows a new vegetation on the prosthesis. Which best explains the negative cultures?
src.explanation: Correct. Culture-negative endocarditis may be due to organisms not recovered by routine microbiology testing or to antimicrobials given before blood cultures were drawn. Her week of antibiotics before any cultures is the clear explanation, and the vegetation keeps endocarditis on the table.

also.explanation: Correct. Culture-negative endocarditis may be due to organisms not recovered in routine microbiology testing or to antimicrobials given before blood cultures. He has taken no antibiotics and had three proper sets drawn, so an organism that routine testing does not recover is the explanation.

items.html: Fungal endocarditis that embolizes. Candida in the blood with a large aortic vegetation is fungal endocarditis, and a cold, blue toe is the expected embolism and occlusion of a larger peripheral artery. Fungal infection is difficult to cure with medication alone, so the definitive step is cardiovascular surgery to replace the valve.
cites: IE Missing Slide and Cases.pptx, Slide 4

src.question: A 24-year-old man who uses intravenous drugs is admitted with 4 weeks of fever. An earlier echocardiogram showed a large aortic valve vegetation. Three blood cultures have grown Candida species, he is receiving fluconazole, and he suddenly develops a cold, blue toe. Which is the appropriate next step?
src.key: Surgery consult for aortic valve replacement
src.explanation: Correct. Candida in three blood cultures with a large aortic vegetation is fungal endocarditis, and fungal infection is difficult to cure with medication alone, which makes it an indication for surgery. The cold, blue toe is the expected complication, embolism and occlusion of a larger peripheral artery, so the definitive step is cardiovascular surgery to replace the valve.

items.html: Vascular phenomena count once. Janeway lesions, conjunctival hemorrhages and septic pulmonary infarcts all belong to ONE minor criterion, vascular phenomena, so together they count once.

src.question: A 33-year-old man who injects drugs has a temperature of 39.2 °C (102.6 °F), painless, flat hemorrhagic spots on his soles, hemorrhages on both conjunctivae and septic pulmonary infarcts on chest imaging. Blood cultures and echocardiography are pending. How many minor modified Duke criteria does he meet?
src.explanation: Correct. Injection drug use (predisposition) and fever are two minor criteria. Janeway lesions, conjunctival hemorrhages and septic pulmonary infarcts all belong to ONE criterion, vascular phenomena, so together they count once. Three minor criteria make the case possible.

items.html: One major plus three minor is definite. An oscillating mass on echocardiography is a major criterion (endocardial involvement); rheumatic mitral regurgitation (predisposition), fever and painful finger-pad nodules (an immunologic phenomenon) are three minor criteria, and one major plus three minor is definite endocarditis.

src.question: A 39-year-old woman who had rheumatic heart disease as a teenager and now has mitral regurgitation has a temperature of 38.6 °C (101.5 °F) and painful, red nodules on several finger pads. Blood cultures are pending, and transesophageal echocardiography shows an oscillating mass on the mitral valve. What is her modified Duke classification?
src.explanation: Correct. The oscillating mass on echocardiography is a major criterion (endocardial involvement). Her rheumatic mitral regurgitation (predisposition), fever of 38.6 °C and painful finger-pad nodules (an immunologic phenomenon) are three minor criteria. One major plus three minor is definite endocarditis.

also.explanation: Correct. The mitral vegetation is a major criterion. Fever, conjunctival hemorrhages (vascular) and a single positive culture that does not meet the major criterion (microbiologic) are three minor criteria. One major plus three minor is definite.

items.html: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and Roth spots in the count. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is on the list of predisposing heart conditions, fever is the fever criterion, and Roth spots are an immunologic phenomenon: three minor criteria make the case possible while cultures and echocardiography are pending.

src.question: A 45-year-old man with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy has a temperature of 38.9 °C (102.0 °F) and white-centered retinal hemorrhages (Roth spots) on fundoscopy. Blood cultures and echocardiography are pending. How many minor modified Duke criteria does he meet?
src.explanation: Correct. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is on the list of predisposing heart conditions, fever of 38.9 °C is the fever criterion, and Roth spots are an immunologic phenomenon. Three minor criteria make the case possible while cultures and echocardiography are pending.

items.html: One major plus two minor is possible. An oscillating mass is a major criterion, and injection drug use and fever are two minor criteria; cultures that are negative because antibiotics were given before they were drawn give no second major criterion. One major plus two minor meets possible (one major and one minor) but not definite.

src.question: A 42-year-old man who injects drugs took 10 days of oral antibiotics from an urgent care clinic for a chest cold before any blood cultures were drawn. He now has a temperature of 38.9 °C (102.0 °F). Three sets of blood cultures show no growth, and transesophageal echocardiography shows an oscillating mass on the tricuspid valve. He has no skin, eye or kidney findings. What is his modified Duke classification?
src.explanation: Correct. The oscillating mass is a major criterion. Injection drug use and fever are two minor criteria. His cultures are negative because antibiotics were given before they were drawn, so there is no second major criterion. One major plus two minor meets possible (one major and one minor) but not definite.

items.html: Suspected endocarditis is managed in hospital. Blood cultures first, then intravenous antibiotics, hospital admission and close monitoring of labs, renal function and cardiovascular status by a multidisciplinary team; stable vital signs do not make it an office problem.

src.question: A 71-year-old woman is seen in the office with 3 weeks of low-grade fever, weight loss, a new murmur and painful red nodules on several finger pads. Her vital signs are stable. Which plan is most appropriate?
src.key: Admit for cultures and intravenous therapy
src.explanation: Correct. Suspected endocarditis is managed in hospital: blood cultures first, then intravenous antibiotics, hospital admission and close monitoring of labs, renal function and cardiovascular status by a multidisciplinary team. Stable vital signs do not make it an office problem.

items.section_title: 7.13 · Prophylaxis: who, which procedures, which drug
items.html: Unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease. Unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease is on the high-risk list, along with prosthetic valves or repair material, previous endocarditis, repaired disease with a residual defect at a prosthetic patch, and transplant valvulopathy; periodontal surgery manipulates the gums, so prophylaxis is given.

src.question: Four adults are booked for periodontal surgery that will manipulate the gums. Which patient needs endocarditis prophylaxis?
src.explanation: Correct. Unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease is on the high-risk list, along with prosthetic valves or repair material, previous endocarditis, repaired disease with a residual defect at a prosthetic patch, and transplant valvulopathy. Periodontal surgery manipulates the gums, so prophylaxis is given.

items.section_title: 7.5 · Clinical manifestations and the peripheral signs
items.html: Ruptured mycotic (infected) aneurysm. Subacute endocarditis is gradually progressive unless it is complicated by a major embolic event or a ruptured mycotic (infected) aneurysm; infective intracranial aneurysms and intracranial hemorrhage are both on the brain's list of complications, and a sudden bleed fits a ruptured aneurysm.

src.question: A 63-year-old man with 6 weeks of subacute endocarditis suddenly develops a severe headache and left-sided weakness. Brain imaging shows an intracranial hemorrhage. Which complication best explains this?
src.explanation: Correct. Subacute endocarditis is gradually progressive unless it is complicated by a major embolic event or a ruptured mycotic (infected) aneurysm, and infective intracranial aneurysms and intracranial hemorrhage are both on the brain's list of complications. A sudden bleed fits a ruptured aneurysm.

items.section_title: 7.16 · Populations: infant, child, adolescent, adult, elderly
items.html: Children: procedures over infected tissue. A prosthetic valve is a high-risk pediatric condition, and prophylaxis is given not only for gum-manipulating dental work and invasive respiratory procedures but also when a procedure is performed over infected skin or musculoskeletal tissue, such as draining an infected abscess.

src.question: A 13-year-old boy with a prosthetic pulmonary valve needs incision and drainage of an infected skin abscess on his forearm. Which is appropriate regarding endocarditis prophylaxis?
src.explanation: Correct. A prosthetic valve is a high-risk pediatric condition, and prophylaxis is given not only for gum-manipulating dental work and invasive respiratory procedures but also when a procedure is performed over infected skin or musculoskeletal tissue. Draining an infected abscess qualifies.

items.html: Four minor criteria is still possible. Injection drug use, fever, septic pulmonary infarcts (a vascular phenomenon) and a single positive culture that does not meet the major criterion are four minor criteria with no major one; three or more minor criteria make the case possible, and definite needs five.

src.question: A 29-year-old woman who injects drugs has a temperature of 39.0 °C (102.2 °F) and a cough, and chest imaging shows septic pulmonary infarcts. One of three blood cultures grows Staphylococcus aureus. Transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography show no vegetation, abscess or new regurgitation. What is her modified Duke classification?
src.explanation: Correct. Injection drug use, fever, septic pulmonary infarcts (a vascular phenomenon) and a single positive culture that does not meet the major criterion are four minor criteria, with no major one. Three or more minor criteria make the case possible; definite needs five.

items.html: Viridans streptococci with chronic kidney disease. Viridans streptococci are treated with penicillin G or ceftriaxone, with or without gentamicin, or with vancomycin; the 2-week regimen that adds gentamicin is only for uncomplicated disease with a rapid response and no chronic kidney disease, so with chronic kidney disease ceftriaxone is given without gentamicin.

src.question: A 74-year-old woman with chronic kidney disease (creatinine 2.7 mg/dL, normal 0.6-1.2) has uncomplicated native mitral valve endocarditis from penicillin-susceptible viridans streptococci and is responding quickly to therapy. Which regimen fits?
src.explanation: Correct. Viridans streptococci are treated with penicillin G or ceftriaxone, with or without gentamicin, or with vancomycin. The 2-week regimen that adds gentamicin is only for uncomplicated disease with a rapid response AND no chronic kidney disease, so with a creatinine of 2.7 mg/dL she gets ceftriaxone without gentamicin.

items.html: What empiric therapy covers. Empiric therapy for endocarditis, started once blood cultures are drawn and before the organism is known, must cover staphylococci, streptococci and enterococci, which is why vancomycin is paired with ceftriaxone (or with gentamicin and cefepime for a prosthetic valve in its first year).

src.question: A 45-year-old man with fever, a new murmur and splinter hemorrhages (thin dark lines under the nails) has three sets of blood cultures drawn, and empiric antibiotics are about to start before any organism is known. Which organisms must the empiric regimen cover?
src.explanation: Correct. Empiric therapy for endocarditis, started once blood cultures are drawn and before the organism is known, must cover staphylococci, streptococci and enterococci, which is why vancomycin is paired with ceftriaxone (or with gentamicin and cefepime for a prosthetic valve in its first year).

items.html: Which patient on antibiotics needs surgery. Heart failure due to valvular dysfunction is the most common indication for surgery, alongside infection not resolving on appropriate antibiotics, abscess and fungal infection; new heart failure from severe regurgitation calls for cardiothoracic surgery evaluation.

src.question: Four patients are on day 5 of appropriate intravenous antibiotics for native valve endocarditis. Which one needs evaluation for surgery?
src.key: New heart failure from severe regurgitation
src.explanation: Correct. Heart failure due to valvular dysfunction is the most common indication for surgery, alongside infection not resolving on appropriate antibiotics, abscess and fungal infection. New heart failure from severe regurgitation calls for cardiothoracic surgery evaluation.

items.html: HACEK organisms in the Duke count. A HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) organism, a typical organism, in two separate cultures is a major criterion; prior endocarditis (predisposition), fever and painful finger-pad nodules (immunologic) are three minor criteria, and one major plus three minor is definite.

src.question: A 56-year-old man who was treated for infective endocarditis 4 years ago has 3 weeks of fever to 38.7 °C (101.7 °F) and painful red nodules on two finger pads. Two separate blood cultures grow Haemophilus species, a HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) organism. Transesophageal echocardiography shows no vegetation, abscess or new regurgitation. What is his modified Duke classification?
src.explanation: Correct. A HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) organism, a typical organism, in two separate cultures is a major criterion. Prior endocarditis (predisposition), fever and painful finger-pad nodules (immunologic) are three minor criteria. One major plus three minor is definite.
